name: Nano Banana
tagline: Browser front end for prompt-driven image generation and photo edits, free tier, no card.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Credit or tier structure not confirmed.

verdictSummary: "Nano banana" is the nickname that stuck to Google's Gemini image model, and sites like this one are chat windows bolted onto that model's API. The window is genuinely a one-sitting build: upload, prompt box, before and after, download, local history. What you cannot build is the model doing the actual editing, so your personal version is a thin client renting the same weights from someone else's datacenter. The honest math is that a free tier with no card beats your own metered API key until you are editing enough images for the per-image cost to matter, at which point owning the client and the key gets cheaper and more private. Call it a weekend win with a permanent third-party dependency stapled to it.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you drop in an image, type a natural-language edit, and get the result back from an image model API with a side-by-side view and a download button.
requirements: An API key for an image generation and editing model, Google Gemini image or OpenAI images
A card on file with the model provider, since metered image APIs are rarely free
Local disk for the image history
whatYouLose: The free tier: your own key is billed per image from the first request
Whatever prompt preprocessing and preset styles the hosted UI adds on top of the raw model
Mobile-friendly polish and fast upload handling on bad connections
Any account, cross-device history, or shareable result links
A fallback when your single provider rate-limits or changes model names underneath you
moatNotes: The moat belongs to the model owner, not to the site wrapping it. Wrappers compete on free credits and speed, which is a race they do not control.
whyPeopleStillPay: Mostly they do not pay, they just use the free tier, which is exactly the point. A hosted wrapper eats the API cost to get your attention, and for someone editing ten images a month that is strictly better than signing up for a cloud billing account and managing a key. The paid tiers sell volume and queue priority to people who have crossed over into real usage, and even those people are paying for convenience rather than capability, since the capability is a public API anyone can call.
notes: The UI here is a weekend; the weights are not, and the weights are the whole product.
prompt:
Build a local-only image editing playground called "banana-bench" in an empty folder.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind. No component library.
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 for edit history. No ORM.
- Images stored on local disk under ./data/images, served through a route handler.
- The model call goes to Google Gemini image generation via @google/genai, key read from GEMINI_API_KEY in .env.local. Write a .env.example with that one line and nothing else.

What it does:
- One page. Drop zone or file picker for a source image, max 10 MB, jpeg/png/webp only.
- A prompt textarea plus a row of preset buttons that just prefill the textarea: "remove the background", "replace the background with a plain studio grey", "make this look like film photography", "remove the object I describe". Presets are text, not special code paths.
- Submit sends the image plus prompt to a POST /api/edit route handler, which calls the model, writes the returned image to disk, inserts a row into SQLite with id, created_at, prompt, source_path, result_path.
- Result view is a side-by-side with a drag slider, plus a Download button and a "use result as new source" button so edits can chain.
- A history strip at the bottom reads from SQLite, newest first, click to reload that pair into the viewer.

Explicitly out of scope: accounts, auth, cloud storage, telemetry, analytics, sharing links, multi-user anything, image upscaling, a mobile app.

Handle the boring parts for real: show the provider's error text when the API rejects a prompt, disable submit while in flight, and never crash the page on a failed request.

Finish with a README that states the actual per-image cost is whatever the provider charges and that this app has no free tier.
